request:
I'm doing HL Economics. We did minimum wages as a price floor this week and my teacher said the textbook diagram is "only half the story" because a famous study in the 1990s found the opposite of what the diagram predicts, and then other economists pushed back on it. I want to understand the actual evidence, not just the diagram. Please answer each part:

(a) Explain, with the diagram described in words, why a minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage in a competitive labour market is predicted to cause unemployment. [4 marks]

(b) Explain what that famous study did and what it found. I want the specifics: who wrote it, which year, which places were compared, which industry, what the minimum wage changed from and to, and roughly what the result was. Then explain who disagreed with it, what data they used instead and what they found. [6 marks]

(c) Explain the monopsony argument that is used to account for the result, and the condition under which a minimum wage could raise employment. [3 marks]

(d) In a town the demand for fast-food labour is Ld = 600 - 40W and the supply is Ls = -100 + 60W, where W is the wage in dollars per hour and L is thousands of workers. Calculate the equilibrium wage and employment, then the employment and the excess supply of labour if a minimum wage of $8 per hour is imposed, then the wage elasticity of demand for labour between those two points, and comment on what it means for the size of the job losses. [6 marks]

(e) To what extent does the evidence undermine the price-floor prediction? [6 marks]

Please say clearly which parts are settled theory and which are still argued about, and say where your figures for the studies come from, because I'll get asked about that if I use them in an essay.
strong_answer_must: Part (a): defines a minimum wage as a legally imposed price floor in the labour market and describes the diagram in order: wage ($ per hour) on the vertical axis, quantity of labour on the horizontal; downward-sloping labour demand (derived from the marginal revenue product of labour), upward-sloping labour supply, equilibrium at We and Le; a floor Wmin above We gives quantity demanded Ld below Le and quantity supplied Ls above Le; the horizontal gap Ls minus Ld is the excess supply of labour (unemployment at the floor). It separates the fall in employment (Le minus Ld) from the excess supply, which also includes workers newly attracted by the higher wage, and says both depend on the elasticities of labour demand and supply.

Part (b): names David Card and Alan Krueger and their 1994 American Economic Review paper on the New Jersey minimum wage rise of 1 April 1992 from $4.25 to $5.05 an hour (about 18.8%), compared with neighbouring eastern Pennsylvania where the minimum stayed at $4.25; the industry is fast-food restaurants (a sample of roughly 410 outlets of chains such as Burger King, KFC, Wendy's and Roy Rogers) surveyed shortly before (February-March 1992) and after (November-December 1992) the rise; the finding is no fall in employment in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania, if anything a small relative rise (the paper's headline is roughly a 13% relative rise in full-time-equivalent employment, about 2.7 FTE per store), with menu prices rising in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania; the work was extended in their 1995 book Myth and Measurement. Card shared the 2021 Nobel memorial prize in economics partly for this natural-experiment work.

Part (b), the dissent: names David Neumark and William Wascher, whose 2000 American Economic Review comment re-examined the same New Jersey-Pennsylvania episode using restaurants' payroll records rather than telephone-survey answers and found employment in New Jersey fell relative to Pennsylvania by roughly 4%; states that Card and Krueger's 2000 reply used official BLS (ES-202) payroll data and reaffirmed no negative employment effect; may add that earlier critics (for example Finis Welch and Daniel Hamermesh in a 1995 Industrial and Labor Relations Review symposium) attacked the survey's measurement error. Each finding is attributed to its authors, the method difference (survey versus payroll data) is stated, and the disagreement is presented as unresolved rather than settled either way.

Part (c): explains monopsony (a single or dominant buyer of labour; the term comes from Joan Robinson, 1933) facing an upward-sloping labour supply, so the marginal cost of hiring an extra worker lies above the wage; the firm hires where the marginal cost of labour equals the marginal revenue product and pays the lower wage read off the supply curve; a minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage (where MRP meets supply) makes the marginal cost of labour flat up to the quantity supplied at that wage and raises both the wage and employment; a minimum above the competitive wage reduces employment as in part (a). May mention the modern search-friction version (Alan Manning's 2003 Monopsony in Motion) that applies to fast food even with many employers.
Part (d), equilibrium: 600 - 40W = -100 + 60W, so 700 = 100W, W* = $7 per hour; L* = 600 - 40(7) = 320 thousand workers, checked against supply (-100 + 60(7) = 320).

Part (d), the floor: at W = $8, Ld = 600 - 320 = 280 thousand and Ls = -100 + 480 = 380 thousand; excess supply = 380 - 280 = 100 thousand workers; employment falls by 320 - 280 = 40 thousand (12.5%); the other 60 thousand of the excess supply are extra workers drawn in by the higher wage, so job losses (40 thousand) are not the same as the unemployment created at the floor (100 thousand).

Part (d), elasticity: percentage change in employment = (280 - 320) / 320 x 100 = -12.5%; percentage change in wage = (8 - 7) / 7 x 100 = +14.29% (one seventh); wage elasticity of demand for labour = -12.5 / 14.29 = -0.875 (to 3 d.p.), so demand is inelastic over this range; states the method used (percentage changes from the original values) and, ideally, that the midpoint (arc) method gives (-40/300) / (1/7.5) = -1.0 and that the total wage bill is unchanged at 7 x 320 = 8 x 280 = $2,240 thousand per hour. Comment: because demand is inelastic, the percentage fall in employment is smaller than the percentage rise in the wage, so job losses are moderate and the earnings of workers who keep their jobs rise more than enough to offset the lost jobs' wages. Units ($ per hour, thousands of workers) appear on every figure.

Part (e): gives an explicit judgement on degree (a verdict phrase such as 'to a limited extent' or 'on balance') and weighs the evidence on both sides with attribution: no detectable job losses in Card and Krueger (1994), Dube, Lester and Reich (2010, contiguous county pairs across state borders), Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer (2019, 'bunching' study of 138 US state-level rises 1979-2016), the UK National Minimum Wage introduced in April 1999 at 3.60 pounds an hour with little employment effect found in Low Pay Commission reviews, and Germany's 8.50 euro minimum of 2015; against negative findings in Neumark and Wascher (2000 and later work), the University of Washington Seattle study (Jardim and others, 2017) finding reduced hours as the city minimum rose towards $13 in 2016, and the 2019 US Congressional Budget Office estimate of a median 1.3 million jobs lost (range zero to 3.7 million) from a $15 federal minimum. Concludes that the theory is settled but the size of the employment effect is the contested empirical question, and that the price-floor prediction holds best for a minimum set high relative to the median wage and in sectors with elastic labour demand.

Throughout: separates settled theory (price floor mechanics, monopsony mechanics, the arithmetic) from contested empirical claims (the sign and size of employment effects), attributes every study and figure to named authors and years, labels figures recalled from memory as such (the gate's 'recalled, not consulted' source tag), ends with a single correctly formatted Sources: line, includes no URLs, and any mark mentioned carries 'provisional' in the same sentence. If it is unsure of a specific (for example the exact sample size), it says so rather than inventing one.
pitfalls: Fabricated or mis-stated study details: wrong authors, wrong year (the wage rose on 1 April 1992; the paper appeared in 1994), wrong states or wrong direction of comparison, wrong amounts (it was $4.25 to $5.05, not $5.25 or $4.75), a precise invented sample size or employment figure, or crediting the payroll-record critique to someone other than Neumark and Wascher.
Presenting Card and Krueger (or Neumark and Wascher) as the settled last word, or inventing a 'consensus' with no attribution; failing to say what data each side used.
Monopsony stated without its condition: a minimum wage raises employment only when set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage; above that it reduces employment.
Treating the whole excess supply (100 thousand) as job losses; the fall in employment is 40 thousand and 60 thousand are new entrants.

Elasticity errors: computing the wage change as 12.5% (dividing by the new wage of $8) instead of 14.29%, dropping the negative sign, giving -1.0 without saying it is the midpoint method, or giving no method at all; omitting units (thousands of workers, $ per hour); arithmetic slips in solving 700 = 100W.
Describing the diagram with goods-market labels (price and quantity of a product) instead of wage and quantity of labour, or saying the minimum wage 'shifts demand'.
Claims about the IB syllabus (for example 'monopsony is an HL-only topic') stated as fact without a source.

Invented current statistics (today's minimum wage levels, current unemployment rates) or invented study figures presented with false precision; URLs; a missing or untagged Sources: line; a mark without 'provisional' in the same sentence.
Part (e) answered without an explicit verdict on degree, or a verdict that ignores the evidence given in part (b).
